Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 34
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.
Restricted configurations found

src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

Explanation

The application is using a Spring Boot version that is not the latest stable release.
Upgrading to the latest stable version ensures you benefit from the newest features, performance improvements, bug fixes, and security patches. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest stable version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose the latest stable Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and identify the latest stable release.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single-deployable Spring Boot 3.5 MVC application that stores photo binaries directly in an Oracle database and serves them through server-rendered Thymeleaf pages and a small JSON upload endpoint.

flowchart TD

Browser["Web Browser - Thymeleaf pages, upload.js"]

end

subgraph App["Application Layer - Spring Boot 3.5.0 on Java 21"]

Web["Spring MVC Controllers"]

Service["PhotoService business logic"]

Views["Thymeleaf templates"]

end

subgraph Data["Data Layer"]

JPA["Spring Data JPA + Hibernate 6.6"]

DB[("Oracle Database XE 21c")]

end

subgraph Infra["Container Infrastructure"]

Compose["Docker Compose - app + oracle-db"]

end

Browser -->|"HTTP GET pages and photos"| Web

Browser -->|"POST /upload, POST /detail/id/delete"| Sec

Web -->|"renders model"| Views

Web -->|"delegates"| Service

Service -->|"CRUD and native queries"| JPA

JPA -->|"SQL over JDBC ojdbc8"| DB

Compose -.->|"runs"| App

Compose -.->|"runs"| DB

~~~

Data Storage & External Services

All data, including photo binaries (@Lob byte[]), lives in a single Oracle photos table. There are no external web services, message brokers, caches or cloud SDKs. The only external system is the Oracle database, run as a sibling container in Docker Compose.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Classic layered design (Controller -> Service -> Repository) with constructor injection and interface-based service.
  • Photos are stored in the database rather than on a file system, so the app container is stateless.
  • Repository queries use Oracle-specific SQL (NVL, ROWNUM, SYSDATE FROM DUAL), tightly coupling the data layer to Oracle.

API & Service Communication Contracts

The application exposes 5 HTTP endpoints from a single deployable service: server-rendered HTML pages, a JSON upload API and a binary photo endpoint. There are no outbound service calls.

Service Catalog

ServicePortCategoryPurpose
photoalbum-java-app (photo-album module)8080BusinessPhoto gallery, upload, detail view, delete
oracle-db (third-party container, Oracle XE 21.3.0)1521 (SQL), 5500 (EM)InfrastructureRelational data store for the app

API Endpoints Inventory

ServiceMethodPathRequest TypeResponse Type
photoalbum-java-appGET/noneHTML view index (model photos)
photoalbum-java-appPOST/upload (auth required)multipart files (list of MultipartFile)JSON map: success, uploadedPhotos, failedUploads; 400 if no files
photoalbum-java-appGET/detail/{id}path idHTML view detail; redirects to / if not found
photoalbum-java-appPOST/detail/{id}/delete (auth required)path id302 redirect to / with flash message
photoalbum-java-appGET/photo/{id}path idBinary image (ByteArrayResource) with stored MIME type; 404 if missing

Management & Observability Endpoints

ServiceEndpointCustom Metrics (if any)
photoalbum-java-appNone (Spring Boot Actuator not included)None

DTOs & Contracts

UploadResult is an internal mutable result object (not serialized directly); the upload endpoint builds Map responses by hand. Photo is the JPA entity and is passed to Thymeleaf views (see data-architecture.md). There are no records, OpenAPI/Swagger specs, protobuf or GraphQL schemas. JSON serialization uses Spring Boot's default Jackson configuration. Multipart limits: 10MB per file, 50MB per request, max 10 files per upload configured.

Communication Patterns

  • Synchronous only: browser to controller over HTTP; controller to service by direct method calls; JPA to Oracle over JDBC.
  • Asynchronous: none (no queues, events or schedulers).
  • Resilience: no circuit breaker, retry or timeout configuration; service failures return an error page redirect or an empty gallery.
  • Service discovery / gateway / load balancing: none; the app reaches the database by the fixed host name oracle-db on the Compose network.
  • Startup dependency chain: the app starts only after the Oracle container is healthy (see configuration-inventory.md).
  • Security posture: HTTP Basic authentication protects POST /upload and POST /detail/*/delete (in-memory ADMIN user, BCrypt). All other endpoints, including photo reads, are public. CSRF is disabled, and no TLS is configured (plain HTTP on 8080).

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. oracle-db starts and runs oracle-init scripts on startup.
  2. oracle-db healthcheck (sqlplus SELECT 1 FROM DUAL; 30s interval, 15 retries, 180s start period) must report healthy.
  3. photoalbum-java-app waits for oracle-db with depends_on: condition: service_healthy, restart: on-failure.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

Operator copies .env.example to .env and sets values; Docker Compose reads .env and injects variables into the Oracle and application containers (Compose fails fast if they are unset); Spring resolves them via property placeholders. No external secret store (Key Vault) is used.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album is a small photo-sharing gallery: users browse photos publicly, while an authenticated admin uploads and deletes images stored in the database.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoGalleryUploaded image with metadata and binary dataStandalone; ordered by uploadedAt for previous/next navigation
UploadResultGalleryOutcome of a single file upload (success, file name, error, photo id)Produced by PhotoService, consumed by HomeController

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
photoalbum-java-appPhoto galleryPhoto, UploadResultOracle database

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload photos

  1. Admin submits one or more files to POST /upload with HTTP Basic credentials.
  2. For each file, PhotoServiceImpl.uploadPhoto validates the MIME type against the allow-list, size against 10MB, and non-empty content.
  3. Image dimensions are read from the header; images above 40 million pixels are rejected.
  4. A Photo (UUID id, upload timestamp) is saved with its bytes to Oracle.
  5. The endpoint returns JSON with uploadedPhotos and failedUploads; partial success is allowed.

Workflow 2: Browse gallery and view detail

  1. GET / lists all photos newest first.
  2. GET /detail/{id} loads a photo and resolves the previous (older) and next (newer) photo ids for navigation.
  3. Images are rendered through GET /photo/{id}, which streams bytes with the stored MIME type.

Workflow 3: Delete photo

  1. Admin posts to /detail/{id}/delete; the photo is looked up and deleted.
  2. The user is redirected to the gallery with a success or "Photo not found" flash message.

Cross-Service Data Flows

Single service; no aggregation across services. All data flows between controllers, service and the Oracle database. If the database is unavailable, the gallery renders empty and detail/photo requests redirect or return 404/500.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Allowed types: image/jpeg, image/png, image/gif, image/webp (from Content-Type header).
  • Maximum file size 10MB; empty files rejected; decoded image limit 40 million pixels.
  • Only authenticated users may upload or delete; viewing is public.
  • Photo ids are random UUIDs; uploadedAt is assigned at creation and drives navigation ordering.
  • Missing MIME type falls back to application/octet-stream in queries.

Version & Compatibility Risks

Spring Boot 3.5.0 and its managed libraries (Spring Framework 6.2.7, Tomcat 10.1.41, Jackson 2.19.0, Spring Security 6.5.0, Logback 1.5.18) are behind current patch releases and have multiple published advisories; see the security assessment. ojdbc8 targets Java 8 (ojdbc11 is recommended for Java 21). Oracle-specific native SQL limits portability to Azure-managed databases such as PostgreSQL.

Notable Observations

  • Versions are almost entirely governed by the Spring Boot parent BOM; only commons-io has an explicit version.
  • commons-io has no usages in the source tree and could be removed.
  • spring-boot-devtools is declared optional and should not ship in production images (the Dockerfile builds a plain jar, so repackaging excludes it).
  • Spring Security was introduced to protect state-changing endpoints.

Photo Album persists all state in one Oracle table (photos) through Spring Data JPA/Hibernate, including the photo binaries stored as a BLOB.

Key Repository Methods

ServiceRepositoryNotable MethodsPurpose
photo-albumPhotoRepositoryfindAllOrderByUploadedAtDesc()Native query, NVL on mime_type, newest first (loads all BLOBs)
photo-albumPhotoRepositoryfindPhotosUploadedBefore(uploadedAt)Native Oracle query with ROWNUM limit 10 for previous navigation
photo-albumPhotoRepositoryfindPhotosUploadedAfter(uploadedAt)Native Oracle query with SYSDATE FROM DUAL for next navigation

Caching Strategy

No caching layer is configured. HTTP responses for photo bytes are marked no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, so every image request reads the BLOB from Oracle.

Data Ownership Boundaries

Single application and single schema; no cross-service data access. The gallery query selects photo_data for every row, which makes page load cost grow with total stored bytes.
